title: Rates of reaction
learningObjective: describe experiments to investigate the effects of changes in surface area of a solid, concentration of a solution, temperature and the use of a catalyst on the rate of a reaction; describe the effects of changes in surface area of a solid, concentration of a solution, pressure of a gas, temperature and the use of a catalyst on the rate of a reaction; explain the effects of changes in surface area of a solid, concentration of a solution, pressure of a gas and temperature on the rate of a reaction in terms of particle collision theory; know that a catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction, but is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction; know that a catalyst works by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy; draw and explain reaction profile diagrams showing Δ H and activation energy; practical: investigate the effect of changing the surface area of marble chips and of changing the concentration of hydrochloric acid on the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid; practical: investigate the effect of different solids on the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution.

sections.title: Rates of reaction
sections.markdown:
Chemical reactions happen at enormously different speeds. Explosions are
over in a fraction of a second; a strip of magnesium fizzes away in a few
moments in acid; iron rusts over days and weeks; and some things that look
like they should react simply never do — a gold coin can sit in the open air
for thousands of years without changing at all. This chapter is about what
controls those speeds: how to measure the [[rate-of-reaction]], how to
change it, and how to explain every change with one idea —
[[collision-theory]].

The chapter runs on two tracks. The **core track** (assessed in both Paper
1C and Paper 2C) covers the experiments that measure rates, the four factors
that change them — surface area of solids, concentration of solutions,
temperature, and the use of a catalyst — and the particle explanations
behind each one. Two core practicals anchor the chapter: following the
reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, and comparing
solid catalysts in the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide solution. The
**chemistry-only track** (Paper 2C) adds reaction profile diagrams showing
∆H and activation energy, and the precise statement of how a catalyst works
by providing an alternative pathway.

One idea organises everything that follows. Reactions occur when particles
collide — but only some collisions lead to a reaction. Every rate change in
this chapter, from powdered marble to a heated acid to a pinch of black
catalyst powder, is a change in how often successful collisions happen. If
you keep asking "how did that change the collisions?", the whole chapter
stays in one piece.

:::prior-knowledge
You have met the pieces this chapter assembles: particle models of solids,
liquids and gases (u1:c01), the mole and concentration calculations in
mol/dm³ (u1:c05 and u1:c06), acids and carbonates reacting to give carbon
dioxide (u2:c16), and — from the last chapter — activation energy and
exothermic reactions (u3:c19). If mol/dm³ dilution arithmetic feels shaky,
revise it before s07, which uses it heavily.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Rate thinking is everywhere outside chemistry: medicine times drug release,
food science fights spoilage, civil engineering predicts concrete setting
and rusting in bridges. The catalytic converter in section 6 is car
engineering and air-quality policy in one device. Physics reuses the same
collision picture for gas pressure and diffusion.
:::

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the command words for this chapter are *describe* (state the
experiment and the observation), *explain* (give the collision-theory
mechanism) and *know* (recall the catalyst definition and pathway wording
exactly). "Describe" earns marks for the method and the result; "explain"
earns nothing without particles, collisions and frequency. Learn the two
catalyst statements word-for-word — they are marked with surprising
strictness.
:::

:::misconception
"Fast reactions are the ones that give out the most heat." Rate and energy
change are independent: the reaction of hydrogen peroxide decomposing on a
catalyst is fast but only gently warming, while rusting releases a
comparable amount of energy per mole yet takes weeks. Rate is about
*collisions per second*, not about the size of ∆H.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.9 rate-measurement items. Before moving on, say
out loud what the rate of a reaction measures, name the four factors that
change it, and state which of them apply only to gaseous reactants. If any
of those three sentences stalls, reread this section before starting s02.
:::

sections.title: Measuring the rate of reaction
sections.markdown:
The [[rate-of-reaction]] is the speed at which the amount of reactant
decreases, or the amount of product increases, during a chemical reaction.
It is measured as a change in the concentration (or amount) of a reactant
or product per unit time — per second, or per minute.

rate of reaction = (change in concentration, volume or mass) ÷ (time)

Because you can follow either side of the equation, there are two families
of measurement. Follow a **reactant disappearing**: the mass of a solid as
it dissolves away, or the concentration of an acid as it is used up. Or
follow a **product appearing**: the volume of gas collected in a syringe,
or the mass lost as a gas escapes an open flask. Whichever quantity you
choose, the arithmetic is the same — divide the change by the time it took.

The choice of what to measure is decided by the reaction itself. A reaction
that gives off a gas invites you to measure gas volume or mass loss; a
reaction that changes colour or opacity invites you to time how long a
marker takes to disappear from view. In the next section you will put this
into practice with the chapter's core experiment, following a gas being
lost from a reacting flask on a balance.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, rate questions are nearly always "calculate the average rate
between…" items. Write the definition chain first: rate = change ÷ time;
identify the change from the data (mass lost, volume collected,
concentration fallen); identify the time interval. Quote units with every
answer — g/s, cm³/s or mol/dm³ per second — because an unnumbered rate
loses the unit mark even when the arithmetic is perfect.
:::

:::misconception
"Rate is a property of the reaction, so it stays the same from start to
finish." Almost no reaction behaves that way. The rate at the start — when
reactant is plentiful — is the fastest the reaction will ever be, and it
falls as reactants are consumed. That is why every rate value must name its
time interval: "0.47 g in the first minute" and "0.20 g in the second"
describe the same reaction at different moments.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.9 rate-measurement items. Define the rate of a
reaction in one sentence, write the rate equation, and give one quantity a
chemist could follow to measure the rate of a metal–acid reaction. Then
predict: for that same reaction, what would you measure if you wanted to
follow the product side instead?
:::

sections.title: Practical: the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid
sections.markdown:
Marble chips are calcium carbonate, and they react with dilute
hydrochloric acid to give carbon dioxide gas — which escapes — while
calcium chloride solution and water stay behind in the flask:

CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)

The measurement trick for this reaction is elegant: the carbon dioxide
leaves the flask, so **the flask gets lighter as the reaction proceeds**.
Put the whole reaction on a balance and the falling reading is a direct
record of gas produced. This is the experiment you will modify three times
in this chapter — with smaller chips (surface area), with more dilute acid
(concentration), and with a warmer acid (temperature) — so the method
deserves exact attention.

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the acid.
:::

The procedure:

- Use a measuring cylinder to measure 25 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ dilute
  hydrochloric acid.
- Add 5.00 g of large marble chips to a conical flask and place a plug of
  cotton wool at the opening of the flask. The cotton wool lets carbon
  dioxide escape during the reaction but stops any acid spitting out. The
  marble is in [[excess]] — some of it will be left over when the acid has
  all been used up.
- Place everything on a balance and reset the balance to zero.
- Add the acid to the marble chips and record the balance reading every
  30 seconds.

The balance reading goes **negative** as the reaction runs, because carbon
dioxide escapes through the cotton wool and the mixture is losing mass.
Plotting mass of carbon dioxide lost against time gives a curve that rises
steeply at first and then flattens — the shape you will spend this chapter
explaining.

**Reading the graph.** The steeper the slope (gradient) of the line, the
faster the reaction. On this experiment's curve, about
0.47 g of carbon dioxide is produced in the first minute, but only about
0.20 g of extra carbon dioxide arrives in the second minute — the reaction
is already slowing. The curve eventually becomes horizontal: the reaction
has stopped because the acid has been used up, while unreacted marble chips
still sit at the bottom of the flask.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, two method details earn marks by name: the **cotton wool**
(lets gas out, stops acid spray, and is why the mass falls without losing
liquid) and the **excess marble** (guarantees the acid is the limiting
reactant, so gas production stops when acid runs out). If asked why the
balance reading falls, answer "carbon dioxide escapes through the cotton
wool" — never "because the reaction loses mass" without naming the gas.
:::

:::misconception
"The balance measures the mass of carbon dioxide inside the flask." It
cannot — the carbon dioxide is the one substance *leaving*. The falling
reading is the mass of gas that has escaped; the flask still contains all
the calcium chloride, the water and the leftover marble. Students who write
"mass of CO₂ in the flask" mislabel the entire y-axis and lose the graph
interpretation marks that follow.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.15 marble-chips method items. Sketch the setup
in words — flask, chips, acid, cotton wool, balance — and state what the
balance reads after 60 seconds and why. Then explain what the cotton wool
prevents, and what would go wrong with an open flask instead.
:::

sections.title: Explaining the shape of the graph
sections.markdown:
The mass-loss curve from the marble-chip experiment is steep at the start
and flattens towards the end. Two tools turn that shape into numbers:
**average rate** over an interval, and the **instantaneous rate** at a
single moment.

The average rate over any time interval is the mass change divided by the
time interval. For this experiment's curve: the first minute gives 0.47 g of
carbon dioxide, so the average rate is 0.47 ÷ 1 = 0.47 g/min; the second
minute adds only 0.20 g, an average of 0.20 g/min; over the first two
minutes together the average is (0.47 + 0.20) ÷ 2 = 0.34 g/min. Averages
over short intervals near the beginning climb towards the true starting
rate.

To find how fast the reaction is going *at* a particular moment, draw the
tangent to the curve at that time and find the tangent's gradient. On the
curve above, the tangent at 5 minutes gives a loss of about 0.05 g per
minute — the instantaneous rate at that point. You are unlikely to be asked
to draw tangents and find rates this way in an exam, but you are expected
to know what the gradient at a point means.

:::key-point
Remember, the marble chips were in [[excess]] — there was more than enough
to react with all the hydrochloric acid. There will still be unreacted
marble chips in the flask at the end.
:::

**Collision theory.** The curve's shape is explained by thinking about the
particles present and how they interact — an idea called
[[collision-theory]]. Reactions can happen only when particles collide, and
not every collision ends in a reaction: many particles simply bounce off
each other. For a reaction to actually happen, the colliding particles must
bring a minimum amount of energy, called the [[activation-energy]].
Collisions with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy are
called [[successful-collision]]s, and only these make product.

In the calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid reaction, particles in the
acid must collide with particles at the *surface* of the marble chips. As
the acid particles get used up, the collision rate decreases — so the
reaction slows. That is the whole shape of the curve in one sentence:
**steepest at the start when acid particles are plentiful, flatter as they
are consumed, horizontal when the acid is exhausted**. The marble is in a
large excess precisely so that its surface area barely changes during the
run — keeping the comparison fair.

:::key-point
If you have studied u2:c16, you may realise that the particles doing the
colliding in the acid are H⁺ ions. A reaction happens when H⁺ ions collide
successfully with the CO₃²⁻ ions in the calcium carbonate. You should not
talk about "HCl molecules colliding with CaCO₃ molecules". If in doubt
about which particles are actually colliding, it is safer to say
**particle**.
:::

The same reaction can be watched from the other side: instead of mass of
gas lost, collect the gas and measure **volume produced** — a gas syringe
on a sealed flask does this. Either method tracks the same reaction, and
both produce curves with the same characteristic shape.

At International GCSE you normally plot graphs of product formed (mass or
volume rising). But you may also meet graphs showing the **fall in
concentration of a reactant** — the acid's concentration starting high and
sinking towards zero. Read such graphs by the same rule, mirrored: where
the falling curve is steepest, the reaction is fastest; the curve becomes
horizontal when the reaction stops, because all the acid has been consumed.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, "explain why the reaction slows down" is a three-step mark
chain: (1) the concentration of acid particles falls as they are used up;
(2) so collisions between acid particles and the marble surface happen less
frequently; (3) so the frequency of successful collisions falls, and the
rate decreases. Write all three links — jumping straight from "less acid"
to "slower reaction" skips the collision step the mark scheme wants.
:::

:::misconception
"Fewer collisions per second means each collision is weaker." The slowing
is about *how often* particles collide, not how hard. As the acid is used
up, fewer acid particles remain in each cm³, so collisions with the marble
surface become rarer — but a collision in minute five carries the same
energy spread as one in minute one. Rate falls because collision frequency
falls; activation energy has not changed.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.11 collision-theory items. State the two
conditions for a collision to be successful, explain why the mass-loss
curve is steepest in the first minute, and name the particles that actually
collide in the acid. Finish by predicting the graph's shape if the marble
were *not* in excess — what would change at the end of the run?
:::

sections.title: Changing the surface area of the reactants
sections.markdown:
The first rate-changing lever is the size of the solid pieces. Repeat the
marble-chip experiment from s03 using **exactly the same quantities of
everything** — same mass of marble (5.00 g), same volume and concentration
of acid (25 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³) — but with **much smaller chips**. The
reaction with the smaller chips happens faster.

Plot both runs on the same axes — mass of carbon dioxide lost against time
— and two facts jump out. First, both curves **finish at the same final
mass** of carbon dioxide, because both experiments started with identical
quantities: the same total amount of acid must make the same total amount
of gas. Second, the small-chip curve **starts steeper and finishes
sooner**: the same chemistry, delivered faster.

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the acid.
:::

:::key-point
If you are going to investigate the effect of changing the size of the
marble chips, it is important that everything else stays exactly the same
to make this a valid (fair) test.
:::

The general statement, for any reaction between a solid and a liquid or
gas: **reactions are faster if the solid is present as many small pieces
rather than a few large ones**. The more finely divided the solid, the
faster the reaction. Powder beats chips; chips beat a single lump.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the surface-area question always carries two marks: **describe**
(smaller pieces → faster reaction, same final volume of gas) and **explain**
(larger surface area in contact with the acid → more particles of the solid
exposed on the surface → collisions can happen more often per second). If
the question says "explain", the particle sentence is the mark — "small
chips react faster" alone scores nothing.
:::

:::misconception
"Smaller chips make more carbon dioxide because they react faster." Final
gas volume is fixed by the *amounts* of reactants, not by how the solid is
divided. Speeding the reaction changes the *time* axis — the curve climbs
faster and stops earlier — but both curves end at exactly the same height
when the same quantities are used. Saying "more gas" converts a rate mark
into an unforced error.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.10 surface-area effect items. Predict the two
visible differences between the big-chip and small-chip curves (start and
finish), then explain the start difference in terms of exposed surface
particles. Finally, name three quantities that must be kept identical for
the test to be fair.
:::

sections.title: Why smaller pieces react faster
sections.markdown:
Picture one big lump of marble, then the same lump split into smaller
pieces. The total amount of marble has not changed — but the amount the
acid can reach has. In the big lump, liquid particles **can't get at the
particles hidden in the middle** of the solid; only the outer skin of the
lump is exposed. Split the lump and far fewer particles are hidden away:
the same marble now presents a much greater [[surface-area]] to the acid.

Only the particles **on the surface** are available for collisions. Splitting
the solid multiplies the surface on which collisions can happen, so the
**frequency of successful collisions increases** — and that, in
[[collision-theory]] terms, is exactly what a faster reaction is. Nothing
about the particles themselves has changed: each collision is as effective
as before. What changed is how many places collisions can happen.

:::key-point
When explaining this, do not only say that there are more collisions — you
must always include the idea of **time**. Say "the particles collide more
frequently" or "there are more collisions per second".
:::

:::misconception
"Powdering the solid weakens the bonds inside it, which is why it reacts
faster." Grinding changes nothing inside the particles: the calcium
carbonate in powder is chemically identical to the calcium carbonate in a
chip. Only the *geometry* changed — more of the same particles now sit at a
surface where acid particles can reach them. Explanations that invent new
chemistry lose the mark that the correct geometry sentence would have won.
:::

**Surface area in the wild: the catalytic converter.** Large surface areas
speed up reactions outside the lab too. A [[catalytic-converter]] in a car
coats expensive metals — platinum, palladium and rhodium — onto a
**honeycomb structure** in a very thin layer, giving the maximum possible
surface area for the exhaust gases to flow through. In the presence of
these metals, harmful substances such as carbon monoxide and nitrogen
oxides are converted into relatively harmless carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
The huge surface area is essential because the gases are in contact with
the converter for only a very short time on their way down the exhaust
pipe — every square metre of exposed catalyst surface does its work in the
seconds available.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the honeycomb is the classic applied surface-area question.
The two-mark answer: the honeycomb structure gives a **very large surface
area** for the exhaust gases to flow past, so many reactions can happen in
the **short time** the gases spend in the converter. Notice the time idea
again — "large surface area" and "short contact time" belong in the same
sentence.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.10 surface-area effect items. Explain, in
collision-theory language, why a powder reacts faster than the same mass
of a single lump. Then explain why a catalytic converter uses a honeycomb
rather than a solid block of metal, and why the exhaust gases' short
journey makes the surface area critical.
:::

sections.title: Changing the concentration of the reactants
sections.markdown:
Repeat the original marble-chip experiment — large chips, same mass (5.00 g),
same acid volume (25 cm³) — but use hydrochloric acid of **half the
concentration**: 25 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ instead of 2.00 mol/dm³. The
reaction is **slower**. On the mass-loss graph, the half-concentration run
is the less steep curve: same chemistry, gentler climb.

Remember, the marble chips were in [[excess]], so the smaller amount of
acid is what limits the gas made. In the original experiment, 25 cm³ of
2.00 mol/dm³ acid was used; in the diluted run, 25 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³
acid. The second flask starts with **half the number of acid particles**
(half as many moles) — so it will eventually produce **half as much carbon
dioxide**. Fewer particles *and* slower delivery: the final level is lower
and the climb is shallower.

In general: **increasing the concentration of the reactants makes the
reaction faster**. A higher concentration packs more acid particles into
each cm³ of solution, so the particles are closer together and **collide
more frequently** — there are more successful collisions between acid
particles and the marble surface every second. Picture the same number of
pinballs in a smaller machine: contacts per second rise without any
single contact becoming more violent.

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the acid.
:::

:::key-point
To calculate the concentration of a diluted acid, look at the proportions
of acid and water in the mixture:

concentration = (volume of hydrochloric acid ÷ total volume of solution)
× original concentration

For a mixture of 12.5 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ acid made up to 25 cm³ with
water: concentration = (12.5 ÷ 25) × 2.00 = 1.00 mol/dm³. The fraction of
the final volume that is actual acid — here one half — multiplies the
original concentration.
:::

:::did-you-know
*Proportional* and *directly proportional* mean the same thing — and both
require a straight line **through the origin**. A straight line that misses
the origin is *linear*, but not proportional. The distinction matters in
this chapter: the rate–concentration line below must pass through (0, 0),
because with no acid there is no reaction at all.
:::

**Practical: rate against concentration.** Run the original experiment
again with the original large marble chips, but vary the acid
concentration — keeping the mass of chips (5.00 g) and the **total volume
of solution (25 cm³)** fixed. Make each dilution by adding distilled water
to the 2.00 mol/dm³ stock acid with the total still 25 cm³: 12.5 cm³ of
acid + 12.5 cm³ of water gives 1.00 mol/dm³ (half); 5 cm³ of acid + 20 cm³
of water gives 0.40 mol/dm³ (one fifth, 5 out of 25).

For each run, record the mass of carbon dioxide lost in the **first
30 seconds** and divide by 30 s — the average rate during the opening
burst. A loss of 0.32 g, for example, gives an average rate of
0.32 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.011 g/s. Using only the first 30 seconds keeps every run's
rate measurement at the same, steepest part of the curve, where
differences between concentrations show most clearly.

**Reading the result.** Plot rate (y-axis) against acid concentration
(x-axis) and draw the line of best fit. The line goes **through the origin
(0, 0)** — with no acid there is no rate — and it is a **straight line**. A
straight line through the origin means the rate is
[[directly-proportional]] to the concentration of the hydrochloric acid:
double the concentration and the rate doubles; triple the concentration and
the rate triples.

:::key-point
Stretching beyond International GCSE: the rate–concentration relationship
is not always this simple. In some reactions the rate is proportional to
the concentration — the reaction is **first order** with respect to that
reactant (the marble-chip case above). In others, changing the
concentration of one reactant has **no effect** on rate — **zero order**.
And in some the rate is proportional to the **square** of the concentration
— **second order**. If you take chemistry further you will meet all three,
and the order of each reactant becomes a measurable property of the
reaction itself. This is enrichment — you do not need reaction orders at
International GCSE.
:::

:::exam-hint
In the exam, "explain why higher concentration gives a faster rate" needs
the full chain: more particles **in the same volume** → particles closer
together → collide **more frequently** → more successful collisions per
second. The phrase "in the same volume" is the concentration-specific
link — omitting it makes the answer indistinguishable from the
surface-area explanation and loses the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Half the concentration means the reaction makes half the gas, so rate and
yield are the same idea." They are separate axes: concentration changes
both the *speed* of gas production and — when the acid is the limiting
reactant — the *total* made. A quarter-strength acid gives a quarter of the
gas, delivered at a quarter of the pace. Answers that say only "slower" or
only "less gas" each capture half the truth and half the marks; the
question usually wants both.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.15 concentration-method items. Calculate the
concentration when 10 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ acid is diluted to 25 cm³. Then
state what is plotted on each axis of the rate–concentration graph, why the
line must pass through the origin, and what doubling the concentration does
to the rate on that line.
:::

sections.title: Changing the temperature of the reaction
sections.markdown:
Do the original marble-chip experiment once more — everything exactly as
before, but with the acid at a **higher temperature**. The reaction gets
faster: the curve is **steeper and finishes sooner**. The same mass of gas
is given off in the end, because the same quantities of everything were in
the mixture — temperature changed the *speed*, not the *amount*.

There are **two factors** to consider when explaining why increasing the
temperature increases the rate, and the exam wants both:

**1. Particles move faster, so they collide more frequently.** Hotter
particles travel faster between collisions, so collisions happen more
often. This is real, but it only accounts for a **small part** of the
increase in rate.

**2. Many more particles exceed the activation energy.** Recall from s04
that a collision only leads to a reaction — a [[successful-collision]] —
when the particles collide with at least the minimum energy called the
[[activation-energy]]. A small increase in temperature produces a **very
large increase** in the number of particles with energy greater than or
equal to the activation energy. It becomes much more probable that two
particles with sufficient energy to react collide with each other, so the
**frequency of successful collisions** rises sharply. This second factor is
the big one.

So the full explanation ranks its causes: slightly more collisions per
second (factor 1), but — far more importantly — a much larger *fraction* of
those collisions now carries enough energy to react (factor 2). If you
remember only one sentence for the exam, make it: **a small temperature
increase causes a large increase in the number of particles with energy
greater than or equal to the activation energy**.

:::key-point
As an approximation, a **10 °C increase in temperature approximately
doubles the rate** of a reaction. This works for quite a lot of the
reactions met in the lab, as long as the temperature stays within a few
tens of degrees of room temperature.
:::

The doubling rule is a useful sanity check and a favourite exam estimate:
warm a reaction from 20 °C to 30 °C and it finishes in about half the time;
from 20 °C to 40 °C and it is roughly four times as fast. It is an
approximation, not a law — say "approximately doubles" and keep the
"as an approximation" qualifier attached.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the two-factor temperature explanation is marked in a strict
order: collision **frequency** increase first (small contribution), then
the **energy** distribution shift — many more particles with energy ≥
activation energy (large contribution). Answers that give only factor 1
typically score 1 of 2; answers that say particles "have more energy"
without linking to the activation-energy threshold score nothing. Draw the
link explicitly: more particles over the threshold → more successful
collisions per second → faster rate.
:::

:::misconception
"Heating the acid makes the particles bigger, or the activation energy
lower." Neither. Heating changes how fast particles move and how many sit
above the activation-energy threshold — the threshold itself is a property
of the reaction, unmoved by temperature. A reaction at 50 °C still demands
exactly the same minimum collision energy as at 20 °C; it simply has far
more collisions that clear the bar.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.11 temperature-effect items. State both factors
linking temperature to rate, and mark which is dominant. Then use the
doubling rule: if a reaction takes 8 minutes at 20 °C, estimate its time at
40 °C. Finally, explain why the final gas volume in the marble-chip
experiment does not change when the acid is warmer.
:::

sections.title: Changing the pressure on the reaction
sections.markdown:
Pressure is the fourth lever — and the only one with a **state-of-matter
condition** attached. Changing the pressure of a reaction whose reactants
are only **solids or liquids** makes almost no difference to the rate.
Increasing the pressure of a reaction where the reactants are **gases**
does speed the reaction up.

Why the difference? In solids and liquids, particles are packed closely
together with hardly any space between them. Squeezing them harder barely
changes their volume, so there is hardly any change in how many particles
occupy a given space — the particles were already as close as they get.

:::key-point
In solids and liquids, particles are packed closely together and there is
hardly any space in between. Increasing the pressure does not change the
volumes of solids or liquids much, so there is hardly any change in the
number of particles in a given volume.
:::

For a **gas**, the story is completely different. A fixed mass of gas is
mostly empty space, and that space is compressible. Increase the pressure
by **squeezing the gas into a smaller volume** and the particles are forced
closer together, so they **collide more frequently**.

The insight that ties this chapter together: for gases, increasing the
pressure is **exactly the same as increasing the concentration**. Both
words describe the same physical fact — more particles per unit volume —
so both produce the same collision-theory consequence: more frequent
collisions, more successful collisions per second, faster reaction. In an
industrial plant, running a gas reaction at high pressure is simply the
concentration lever operated with a compressor.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the pressure question is almost always a comparison pair:
"why does pressure affect gaseous reactions but not reactions of solids or
liquids?" Answer both halves — gases have mostly empty space, so
compressing them packs particles closer and increases collision frequency;
solids and liquids are already tightly packed, so pressure hardly changes
their particle spacing. One half without the other loses the second mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Increasing pressure squeezes the particles themselves into smaller
shapes." Pressure never compresses the particles — it compresses the
*space between* them. Particles stay the same size in every state and at
every pressure; only their spacing changes. Descriptions of particles being
"crushed" or "squashed smaller" contradict the particle model itself and
void the explanation.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.10 pressure-effect items. State which state of
matter responds to pressure changes and why, then explain the equivalence
"increasing gas pressure = increasing gas concentration" in one sentence of
collision theory. Finish by predicting the effect of doubling the pressure
on the rate of a reaction between two gases — and on the rate of marble
chips dissolving in acid under pressure.
:::

sections.title: Catalysts
sections.markdown:
A [[catalyst]] is a substance that **increases the rate of a reaction but is
chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction**. Learn that definition
exactly — both halves get tested. Because catalysts are not consumed, a
small amount of catalyst can process a huge amount of reactant, and each
reaction has its own preferred catalyst: different reactions need different
catalysts.

The chapter's working example is the decomposition of
[[hydrogen-peroxide]] solution. Hydrogen peroxide is unstable and slowly
breaks down into water and oxygen:

2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g)

Left alone, it decomposes so slowly that only a trace of bubbles appears.
Add a pinch of black manganese(IV) oxide powder — MnO₂, also called
manganese dioxide — and oxygen streams off immediately. Lead(IV) oxide,
PbO₂, also catalyses this decomposition. Manganese(IV) oxide is what is
normally used in the lab for this reaction.

Notice what the equation does *not* contain: the catalyst. Catalysts are
never written into the equation, because they are chemically unchanged at
the end. If you want to show one, write its name or formula **over the top
of the arrow**.

**Bombardier beetles** run this chemistry for a living. The beetle defends
itself by spraying a hot, unpleasant liquid at attackers: it pumps hydrogen
peroxide into a chamber with the enzyme **catalase**, which decomposes it
into water and oxygen — almost explosively, releasing a lot of heat. An
[[enzyme]] is a biological catalyst, and the same catalase can be found in
potatoes and in liver tissue: drop a slice of either into hydrogen peroxide
and it fizzes.

:::key-point
The reaction here is an exothermic reaction: the products have lower energy
than the reactants.
:::

**Proving "chemically unchanged".** Looking the same proves nothing — the
powder could have lost mass. The test is by **weighing**: weigh the
manganese(IV) oxide before adding it to the hydrogen peroxide, then
separate, dry and reweigh it at the end. Filter the mixture through a
**weighed filter paper**, allow the paper and residue to dry, and reweigh.
The mass of manganese(IV) oxide you recover equals the mass you started
with. Speeding up *and* unchanged: both halves of the definition
demonstrated.

**Practical: comparing solid catalysts (spec 3.16).** Measure how the
volume of oxygen produced changes with time, using a gas syringe on a
sealed flask:

:::safety
Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the solution.
:::

- Measure 100 cm³ of 2 vol hydrogen peroxide and transfer it to a 250 cm³
  conical flask.
- Weigh out 0.20 g of manganese(IV) oxide on a balance.
- Add the manganese(IV) oxide to the hydrogen peroxide and quickly replace
  the bung, with the [[gas-syringe]] already attached. Swirl the reaction
  mixture at a constant speed.
- Record the volume of oxygen produced every 20 seconds for 3 minutes and
  plot volume of oxygen against time.
- Repeat with 0.20 g of lead(IV) oxide and 0.20 g of copper(II) oxide,
  keeping everything else the same.

The results show manganese(IV) oxide is a **very effective** catalyst for
this decomposition — the volume–time curve climbs steeply to its final
level. Lead(IV) oxide is **less effective**: the same final volume of
oxygen arrives, but the curve is much shallower. Copper(II) oxide is **not
a catalyst** for this reaction at all — its curve barely leaves the axis.
Same equation, three very different helpers: catalytic activity is
substance-specific.

The decomposition itself is exothermic — the products (water and oxygen)
have lower energy than the reactants — so the flask warms slightly as the
oxygen pours off.

:::did-you-know
*Vol*, meaning volume, is a measurement of concentration used for hydrogen
peroxide. 1 cm³ of 2 vol hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes completely
to give 2 cm³ of oxygen. So "2 vol" tells you the oxygen yield directly —
100 cm³ of 2 vol solution can deliver 200 cm³ of gas.
:::

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the catalyst-confirmation question always wants **two**
pieces of evidence: (1) the reaction is faster than without the candidate
solid, and (2) the solid is recovered **unchanged** — same mass, by
filtering through weighed filter paper, drying and reweighing. Providing
only "it makes bubbles come faster" answers half the definition. And when
asked where a catalyst appears in the equation, the answer is: it doesn't
— or above the arrow, never with the reactants or products.
:::

:::misconception
"A catalyst is used up slowly, which is why industrial plants top it up."
A catalyst that were consumed would be a reactant. Catalysts are chemically
unchanged at the end — they may look dirtier, clump, or be **poisoned** by
impurities, which is why plants replace them — but consumption by the
reaction itself is ruled out by definition. The reweighing experiment in
this section is exactly the evidence that settles the question.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.16 catalytic-decomposition items. Write the
decomposition equation, state the two observations that identify a
substance as a catalyst, and describe the weighing sequence that proves the
second observation. Then predict the three volume–time curves (MnO₂, PbO₂,
CuO) and what their final levels have in common.
:::

sections.title: How does a catalyst work?
sections.markdown:
Not all collisions result in a reaction. Collisions have to involve at
least a certain minimum amount of energy — the [[activation-energy]]. If a
reaction is slow, it means very few collisions carry that much energy:
when most collisions happen, the particles simply bounce off each other.

A [[catalyst]] works by **providing an alternative route (pathway) for the
reaction, involving a lower activation energy**. With a lower activation
energy on the alternative route, many more collisions are successful: far
more particles now have energy greater than or equal to the activation
energy *for that route*. The particles' own energy has not changed — it has
been made **easier for them to react**.

**The mountain-and-tunnel picture.** Imagine two valleys separated by a
mountain. Only a few very energetic people will climb over the mountain
from one valley to the next. Now build a road tunnel through the mountain:
lots of people can now travel easily between the valleys. The tunnel is the
catalyst's alternative route — the mountain was never lowered, but the
journey no longer requires climbing it.

**Phrasing the answer precisely.** Say: *"Catalysts provide an alternative
route with a lower activation energy."* They do **not** "lower the
activation energy" — any more than building a tunnel lowers the mountain.
The original route still exists, and particles that collide with enough
energy still use it, just as the most energetic climbers can still go over
the top. The mark scheme guards this wording: "lower activation energy"
alone describes a different (wrong) picture; "alternative pathway with
lower activation energy" is the required statement.

:::misconception
"A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the reaction." The reaction's
uncatalysed route keeps its original activation energy. The catalyst adds
a **new route** whose activation energy is lower — that is what "provide an
alternative pathway" means. The tunnel analogy earns its keep here: the
mountain's height never changed; a easier way through appeared.
:::

**Reaction profile diagrams (Paper 2C).** A [[reaction-profile]] diagram
puts **energy on the vertical axis** and the **progress of the reaction on
the horizontal axis**. The reactants sit on a level at the left, the
products on a level at the right, and between them the energy rises to a
maximum — the top of the hill that colliding particles must clear. Two
measured quantities live on this diagram:

- The **activation energy** is the vertical distance from the reactants'
  level **up to the top of the hill**.
- The **enthalpy change ∆H** is the vertical distance from the reactants'
  level **down to the products' level** (down for exothermic, where the
  products end lower).

**Drawing the catalysed profile.** To show the effect of a catalyst, draw a
second curve on the same diagram: a **lower hill** between the same two
levels. Adding a catalyst gives the reaction an alternative way to happen
with a lower activation energy — the new curve's peak sits below the
original one. Label both activation energies (Ea without catalyst, the
smaller Ea with catalyst) with arrows from the reactants' level to each
peak. The reactants' and products' levels are identical on both curves:
same starting chemistry, same ending chemistry, easier journey.

:::key-point
Notice that the difference in energy between the reactants and the products
remains the same with or without a catalyst.
:::

That equality is the diagram's deepest fact. The catalyst changed the
*route*, never the *destination*: ∆H is fixed by the reactants' and
products' energy levels, and those levels belong to the chemicals, not to
the pathway. This is why a catalyst speeds a reaction without changing the
energy change — and why it cannot make an impossible reaction possible, or
shift the position of equilibrium. Route, not destination.

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the reaction-profile diagram is marked on labels: both axes,
both energy levels, an arrow for activation energy (reactants → peak) and
an arrow for ∆H (reactants → products). The catalyst version adds a second,
lower curve — and the commonest lost mark is forgetting that **∆H must be
identical on both curves**. If asked "why?", answer: the energy difference
depends only on the reactants and products, which the catalyst does not
change.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.14C reaction-profile items. Sketch the
exothermic reaction profile from memory: axes, reactant level, product
level, ∆H arrow, activation-energy arrow. Add the catalysed curve and mark
which quantity shrank and which stayed put. Then write the catalyst
statement in its exact mark-scheme form — and its forbidden contraction.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 20 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete rate toolkit: the rate definition and its
measurement by mass loss or gas volume; the marble-chip experiment and its
graph, with average rates and tangents; collision theory with its
successful-collision condition; and the four levers — surface area,
concentration, temperature and catalysts — each explained by the same
particle picture. For Paper 2C you can also draw reaction profile diagrams
showing ∆H and activation energy, including the catalysed profile with its
lower alternative route. The question bank for this chapter joins the
platform by the specification points below, so every practice item you are
served targets exactly the skills these sections taught.

Before you open the question bank, audit yourself against the chapter's
core moves. Can you read a mass-loss curve — steepness, final level, when
it flattens, and why? Can you explain each of the four levers in one
collision-theory sentence with *frequency* and *per second* attached? Do
you carry the catalyst definition and the alternative-pathway wording
word-for-word? On the Paper 2C track: can you draw both reaction profiles
and say which quantity the catalyst changed and which it did not? Anything
that wobbled is a section to revisit, not a reason to start over.

:::summary
- **[[rate-of-reaction]]**: change in concentration, volume or mass per
  unit time; measured by mass loss (balance + cotton wool) or gas volume
  (gas syringe). Rate = change ÷ time; the steepest part of the curve is
  the fastest the reaction is ever going to be.
- **[[collision-theory]]**: reactions happen only when particles collide
  with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy — a successful
  collision. Rate changes are changes in the frequency of successful
  collisions, always stated per second.
- **Surface area**: more finely divided solid → more particles exposed at
  the surface → more collisions per second → faster; same final gas volume.
  Honeycomb catalytic converters apply the same idea to exhaust gases.
- **Concentration**: more particles in the same volume → closer together →
  collide more frequently → faster. For marble chips + HCl the rate is
  directly proportional to acid concentration (straight line through the
  origin); dilution arithmetic = (acid volume ÷ total volume) × original
  concentration.
- **Temperature**: particles collide slightly more often, but the dominant
  effect is many more particles with energy ≥ activation energy — a small
  temperature rise causes a large rate rise; roughly, +10 °C ≈ double the
  rate near room temperature.
- **Pressure**: gases only — squeezing a gas into a smaller volume is
  concentration-in-disguise; solids and liquids are already tightly packed,
  so pressure changes almost nothing.
- **Catalysts**: increase the rate but are chemically unchanged at the end
  (prove it by weighing before and after filtering); work by providing an
  alternative pathway with lower activation energy — never "lower the
  activation energy". ∆H is identical with or without the catalyst.
- **Paper 2C profiles**: energy vs reaction progress; activation energy =
  reactants → peak; ∆H = reactants → products; the catalysed curve is a
  lower hill between unchanged levels.
:::

:::can-you
- Define the rate of a reaction and calculate an average rate from mass or
  volume data?
- Describe the marble-chip experiment — apparatus, cotton wool, excess,
  balance readings — and sketch the shape of its graph?
- State the two conditions for a successful collision and use them to
  explain why reactions slow down as reactants are used up?
- Explain all four rate levers (surface area, concentration, temperature,
  catalyst) in collision-theory language, with frequency and per-second
  wording?
- State and prove the catalyst definition, including the unchanged-mass
  test by filtration and reweighing?
- Estimate rate changes with the 10 °C doubling rule, keeping the
  approximation qualifier?
- Draw and label an exothermic reaction profile showing ∆H and activation
  energy — and add the catalysed curve with both activation energies
  (Paper 2C)?
:::

:::exam-hint
Past-paper items for this chapter cluster into three question shapes: a
graph-interpretation item (describe the curve, calculate an average rate,
read a tangent), a describe-and-explain pair on one of the four levers
(the "explain" mark always wants the collision mechanism with frequency
wording), and the catalyst block — definition, proof of unchanged mass, and
the Paper 2C profile diagram. Practise all three shapes against the clock,
and keep the chapter's discipline: description first, particles second,
*per second* always.
:::

:::misconception
"Learning the four effects is enough for this chapter." The effects are the
predictable half. The unpredictable half is the *shape* of the
explanations: which mass goes into an average rate, why the line of best
fit must pass through the origin, why temperature's two factors are not
equal partners, why the catalyst changes Ea but never ∆H. The examiner
tests the mechanism behind every effect; the sections of this chapter were
written so each mechanism is one sentence you can quote.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.9–3.16 chapter assessment items. Work through
the can-you list honestly, marking each item secure or shaky, then take the
platform's spec-joined question set for 3.10 and 3.11 first — the
explain-the-effect questions earn the most marks per minute of revision,
and they all run on the same collision sentence.
:::
